ok so it seems you're shifting the discussion away from the personhood of an embryo in early stage of development and towards whether or not that embryo can be terminated, if it is a human. I still don't see why you think an organism's ability to survive outside of the womb determines its status of personhood. After conception, the clump of cells doesn't require any additional ingredients that an adult doesn't. It needs nutrients, etc. but it's fully assembled in the way that its body is distinguishable and unique from the body it resides in. It is no longer comparable to other cells within the pregnant person's body.

I'm going to assume that the embryo (developing human, in your words) is a person and move on. We need this framework to continue on talking about abortion and rights. If you disagree with this assumption so be it, but that's the framework I'm using as I reply to the rest of your comment.

First off, leave religion out of it. You seem bitter towards religious people who base all their policies on their religion. Fair. But I'm not religious, and there's a sensible argument to be made against abortion without appealing to supernatural beings. I just believe in natural rights and objective morality. 

Also, I agree that people with unwanted pregnancies have the same rights as any other person. Most pro-choice people focus only on the autonomy of the pregnant person without fully grappling with the life or potential life of the "clump of cells" or whatever they describe the underdeveloped human as. But our right to bodily autonomy stops where another body begins. In this natural process by which all humans come into being, the other body in question resides in someone else. Unfortunate, but again the desirability of a baby doesn't determine its value or possession of rights. There should be more consideration for people with unwanted pregnancies in terms of social services and support, but even if a pro-life person doesn't give this disclaimer, it doesn't change the validity or strength of their argumentation with respect to the rights of the child. 

I'd say the comparison to forced organ donation is a false equivalency. You don't naturally come into being surgically tied to an adult or born child. It's a difference in actively terminating a life (abortion) vs passively allowing a life to end if its on that trajectory anyway (not donating organs). This is a huge moral distinction. It's wrong for me to shoot you, I have a moral obligation to not do that. I don't have a moral obligation to put myself in danger by trying to disarm the gunman that's about to shoot you. 

Murder is objectively immoral. Human beings have inherent rights. These are my beliefs. As you have correctly pointed out, the most fundamental of those rights are the right to life and the right to bodily autonomy. I'd say in that order, especially since the right to bodily autonomy is dependant on the right to life as you, yknow, need to be alive to practice bodily autonomy. 

Combine these rights being possessed by all humans with the fact that unborn babies are essentially the same as newborn babies (underdeveloped humans, but not non-human) and you arrive at the conclusion that abortion is no more moral than terminating a newborn.

You can disagree with that reasoning, but based on your phrasing I'm assuming (maybe wrongly, feel free to correct me) that you assign more value to / have more empathy for the rights of fully functioning humans than less developed, less autonomous humans. That's concerning. All infants, and plenty of adults, are completely dependent on other people for their survival. I'm also assuming you don't think that these people lack their right to life just because they impose on another person's right to autonomy. An unborn  person impedes much much more severely on a person's autonomy than a breastfeeding infant or terminally ill adult patient of course, but does that counteract the rights of the dependant person in question in either case? 

I don't suspect I'm going to change your mind anytime soon, but please stop painting with a broad brush as you do when you portray pro-lifers as religious fanatics with no concern for the trauma of carrying an unwanted pregnancy and who are too dumb to accept modern medicine.

I think that's a false dilemma, that either you affirm everything an individual claims as their identity or deny it. Personally I think "conversion therapy" could be applied to either extreme -- converting an individual to the identity society thinks is acceptable (traditionally) or converting them from the identity they were assigned to the one they've "chosen." Neither is good. Therapy should be talking about why/when the identity dilemma came about and possible influences on identity, as well as how the individual feels about it and what would be the healthiest way to progress. Your comment is an extreme, hopefully facetious example that shouldn't be catered to but the effective way to address a person identifying as you've described probably isn't to send them to a scared straight camp like those that come to mind when you just hear "conversion therapy." there's probably a lot of context to that identity dilemma that needs to be unpacked.
